cards.front: In the JavaFX theater metaphor, name the container chain from window down to the rendered tree.
cards.extra: The platform builds the Stage (the window). You supply a Scene holding a root node, and that root anchors the tree of Nodes the runtime renders. The metaphor is stage, scene, cast.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.StackPane root = new javafx.scene.layout.StackPane();
javafx.scene.Scene scene = new javafx.scene.Scene(root, 300, 200);   // root of the scene graph
javafx.stage.Stage stage = new javafx.stage.Stage();
stage.setScene(scene);   // Stage holds the Scene, which holds the scene graph
stage.show();

cards.front: Which thread must construct and modify a JavaFX Stage and its scene objects?
cards.extra: JavaFX, like Swing, is a single-threaded UI model. Long-running work belongs on background threads; only the code that touches the scene graph must run back on the FX thread, which is why JavaFX ships a concurrency API.
cards.example:
javafx.application.Platform.runLater(() -> {
    javafx.stage.Stage stage = new javafx.stage.Stage();   // construct and modify the Stage here
    stage.setTitle("JavaFX Application Thread");
});
System.out.println("UI work runs on the JavaFX Application Thread");

cards.front: How many parents may a JavaFX Node have, and how many scenes may it belong to?
cards.back: Exactly one parent; one scene at a time
cards.extra: Only the root node is parentless. A node participates in rendering only once added to the scene graph, and it cannot be in two scenes — you must remove it before adding it elsewhere.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.Label node = new javafx.scene.control.Label("X");
javafx.scene.layout.VBox first = new javafx.scene.layout.VBox(), second = new javafx.scene.layout.VBox();
first.getChildren().add(node);   // exactly one parent
second.getChildren().add(node);  // removed from first: still only one parent
javafx.scene.Scene scene = new javafx.scene.Scene(first, 200, 100);
System.out.println(node.getParent() == second && node.getScene() == scene);   // one scene at a time

cards.front: In JavaFX's 2D coordinate system, where is the origin and which way do the axes grow?
cards.back: Upper-left origin; x grows right, y grows down
cards.extra: JavaFX uses an absolute coordinate system plus local systems relative to each parent, both anchored at the parent's upper-left corner. A z-axis adds depth for 3D.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle r = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(0, 0, 10, 10);
System.out.println(r.getX() + "," + r.getY());   // 0,0: upper-left origin
r.setX(20); r.setY(20);   // x grows right, y grows down
System.out.println(r.getX() + "," + r.getY());   // 20,20

cards.front: What parent type manages children but provides no layout capability?
cards.extra: Group places every child at the origin (0,0) using default alignment — text is anchored at its bottom-left, shapes are centered — so content ends up clipped. Use layout panes instead and let them react to resizes.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.Group group = new javafx.scene.Group();
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle r = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(10, 10, 20, 20);
group.getChildren().add(r);   // Group manages children but provides no layout
System.out.println(group.getChildren().size() + " " + r.getX());

cards.front: Which class is the entry point the JavaFX runtime instantiates and whose start() it invokes?
cards.extra: The runtime constructs your Application subclass and the primary Stage, then calls your overridden start(Stage) — you never call main's logic yourself in a JavaFX app.
cards.example:
class Demo extends javafx.application.Application {
  public void start(javafx.stage.Stage stage) { stage.setTitle("Demo"); stage.show(); }
}
// the JavaFX runtime instantiates Demo, a subclass of Application, and invokes start()

cards.front: AWT/Swing Rectangle and JavaFX Rectangle clash — what package rule keeps the imports straight?
cards.extra: JavaFX shares many class names with AWT/Swing (Rectangle, Text, Button). Importing from javafx.scene.* avoids silently binding to the wrong widget.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle fx = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(10, 10, 40, 20);
java.awt.Rectangle awt = new java.awt.Rectangle(10, 10, 40, 20);   // same simple name, different package
System.out.println(fx.getWidth() + " " + awt.getWidth());   // JavaFX classes live under javafx.*

cards.front: In JavaFX, what can a Shape's fill property be set to?
cards.extra: Thankfully a shapes' fill is a Paint, so a gradient (built by interpolating color stops) or an image pattern can replace a flat Color.LIGHTBLUE.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.shape.Shape shape = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(40, 40);
shape.setFill(javafx.scene.paint.Color.BLUE);   // a Color
shape.setFill(new javafx.scene.paint.RadialGradient(0, 0, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, true, javafx.scene.paint.CycleMethod.NO_CYCLE, new javafx.scene.paint.Stop(0, javafx.scene.paint.Color.WHITE), new javafx.scene.paint.Stop(1, javafx.scene.paint.Color.BLUE)));   // radial (linear works too)
shape.setFill(new javafx.scene.paint.ImagePattern(new javafx.scene.image.Image("file:///tile.png")));   // an image

cards.front: In JavaFX Color alpha, what do 1.0 and 0.0 mean?
cards.extra: Alpha is the fourth channel alongside red, green and blue. A value like 0.5 shows the color while letting whatever is behind it bleed through.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.paint.Color opaque = new javafx.scene.paint.Color(1, 0, 0, 1.0);
javafx.scene.paint.Color clear = new javafx.scene.paint.Color(1, 0, 0, 0.0);
System.out.println(opaque.getAlpha() + " " + clear.getAlpha());   // 1.0 opaque, 0.0 transparent

cards.front: What does Text add over a plain Shape in JavaFX?
cards.back: Font, text alignment, wrap width, and the string
cards.extra: Text extends Shape, so it inherits fill, stroke and effects, then adds text-specific properties. The constructor takes the string; setFont() picks the typeface.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.text.Text text = new javafx.scene.text.Text("Hello");   // Text extends Shape and holds the string
text.setFill(javafx.scene.paint.Color.BLUE);   // inherited Shape fill
text.setFont(javafx.scene.text.Font.font(18));
text.setTextAlignment(javafx.scene.text.TextAlignment.CENTER);
text.setWrappingWidth(120);
System.out.println(text.getText() + " " + text.getFont().getSize() + " " + text.getWrappingWidth());

cards.front: Which JavaFX layout control matches: "stacks children back-to-front in insertion order, centered by default"?
cards.extra: First child added is drawn first, so it sits behind later children — add the background shape before the label, or the shape hides it. Per-node alignment and margin can be set through the pane's static setters.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.StackPane stack = new javafx.scene.layout.StackPane();
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle back = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(40, 40);
javafx.scene.text.Text front = new javafx.scene.text.Text("front");
stack.getChildren().addAll(back, front);   // back-to-front in insertion order, centered by default
System.out.println(stack.getChildren());

cards.front: FlowPane vs TilePane — what is the difference in cell sizing?
cards.extra: Both wrap children along a configurable boundary (horizontal by default). FlowPane's cells follow node size, so mixed-size content flows naturally; TilePane forces a uniform grid.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.FlowPane flow = new javafx.scene.layout.FlowPane();
javafx.scene.layout.TilePane tile = new javafx.scene.layout.TilePane();
flow.getChildren().add(new javafx.scene.control.Label("a much longer label"));
tile.getChildren().add(new javafx.scene.control.Label("a much longer label"));
System.out.println("FlowPane: variable cells; TilePane: equal cells");

cards.front: Which layout pane anchors children to a pane edge at a configurable pixel offset, surviving resizes?
cards.extra: You set an offset from each edge per child, and the pane re-applies those anchors when the container resizes — making it a common top-level manager for margins.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.AnchorPane pane = new javafx.scene.layout.AnchorPane();
javafx.scene.control.Button ok = new javafx.scene.control.Button("OK");
pane.getChildren().add(ok);
javafx.scene.layout.AnchorPane.setTopAnchor(ok, 12.0);
javafx.scene.layout.AnchorPane.setLeftAnchor(ok, 20.0);
pane.resize(400, 300);   // anchors are re-applied on resize: 12 px from top, 20 px from left

cards.front: What are the five named regions of a BorderPane?
cards.extra: Each region is optional. The center area defaults to center alignment while top defaults to left, so a centered title needs an explicit Pos.CENTER.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.BorderPane pane = new javafx.scene.layout.BorderPane();
pane.setTop(new javafx.scene.control.Label("Top")); pane.setBottom(new javafx.scene.control.Label("Bottom"));
pane.setLeft(new javafx.scene.control.Label("Left")); pane.setRight(new javafx.scene.control.Label("Right"));
pane.setCenter(new javafx.scene.control.Label("Center"));   // the five named regions
System.out.println(pane.getChildren().size());

cards.front: What makes GridPane different from HBox/VBox?
cards.back: It lays out in a 2D grid with row/column spans
cards.extra: Row height is uniform across a row and column width uniform across a column, but nodes may span several cells. Cells are addressed by column and row index, with optional span arguments.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.GridPane grid = new javafx.scene.layout.GridPane();
grid.add(new javafx.scene.control.Label("A"), 0, 0, 2, 1);   // column 0, row 0, spanning 2 columns
grid.add(new javafx.scene.control.Label("B"), 0, 1);
System.out.println(grid.getChildren());   // 2D grid with row/column spans

cards.front: What special capability does SplitPane add over a plain pane?
cards.extra: SplitPane carves its space into horizontally or vertically arranged areas separated by a draggable divider, and you usually nest other panes inside each area.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.SplitPane split = new javafx.scene.control.SplitPane();
split.getItems().addAll(new javafx.scene.control.Label("left"), new javafx.scene.control.Label("right"));
System.out.println(split.getItems().size() + " areas, " + split.getDividers().size() + " movable divider");

cards.front: Changing the Scene's width/height or fill requires what constructor arguments?
cards.back: Root node, width, height, and an optional fill color
cards.extra: new Scene(root, 350, 230, Color.LIGHTYELLOW) — the root defines the scene graph, the dimensions set the viewport, and the third argument paints the background.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.StackPane root = new javafx.scene.layout.StackPane();
javafx.scene.Scene plain = new javafx.scene.Scene(root, 400, 300);   // root, width, height
javafx.scene.Scene filled = new javafx.scene.Scene(root, 400, 300, javafx.scene.paint.Color.LIGHTBLUE);   // optional fill
System.out.println(plain.getWidth() + " " + filled.getFill());

cards.front: What decides where a layout pane puts each child?
cards.back: The pane's own rules plus your configured constraints
cards.extra: Each pane type has a placement policy (stacking, grid cells, anchors, flow) and exposes per-pane and per-node settings — alignment, margin, span — that refine it.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.HBox box = new javafx.scene.layout.HBox();
javafx.scene.control.Label label = new javafx.scene.control.Label("x");
javafx.scene.layout.HBox.setHgrow(label, javafx.scene.layout.Priority.ALWAYS);   // constraint you configure
box.getChildren().add(label);   // the pane's own rule places children left to right
System.out.println(javafx.scene.layout.HBox.getHgrow(label));

cards.front: JavaFX property listeners: invalidation vs change — what does each provide?
cards.back: Invalidation: notified, no values; change: old + new value
cards.extra: An invalidation listener only learns the value went stale; it must read the property (or call the getter) to see the new value. A change listener is handed observable, oldValue and newValue, so it costs more to maintain.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty p = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty(1);
p.addListener((javafx.beans.Observable o) -> System.out.println("invalidated: no values"));
p.addListener((javafx.beans.value.ObservableValue<? extends Number> o, Number oldV, Number newV) -> System.out.println("changed: " + oldV + " -> " + newV));
p.set(2);

cards.front: Why must an invalidation listener cast the Observable it receives?
cards.extra: The listener signature hands you Observable, not ObservableValue<T>, so getting at the concrete value needs a downcast — or skip the observable entirely and call the property's getter such as getStatus().
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty status = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty("idle");
status.addListener(o -> {
    String value = ((javafx.beans.value.ObservableValue<String>) o).getValue();   // o is a non-generic Observable
    System.out.println(value);
});
status.set("busy");

cards.front: After a.bind(b), what happens if you call a.set(...)?
cards.back: It throws — a bound property cannot be set
cards.extra: You must unbind() first. The bound property is now driven by its source, so an explicit set would silently be overwritten or rejected.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty a = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty(1);
javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty b = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty(2);
a.bind(b);
try { a.set(9); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("bound: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }
System.out.println(a.get());   // 2: a bound property cannot be set

cards.front: bind() vs bindBidirectional() regarding explicit set() calls?
cards.back: bind(): setting fails; bindBidirectional(): setting is allowed
cards.extra: Unidirectional binding takes full control of the target. A bidirectional pair is a live two-way mirror, so either side may be set and the other follows.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty a = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty(1.0), b = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty(2.0), c = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty(3.0);
a.bind(b); c.bindBidirectional(b);
// a.set(9.0) fails; c.set(9.0) is allowed and updates b
c.set(9.0);
System.out.println(a.get() + " " + c.get() + " " + b.get());   // 2.0 9.0 9.0

cards.front: For a.bindBidirectional(b), which side's value wins as the shared initial value?
cards.extra: Bidirectional binding is not symmetric at creation: both properties adopt the argument's current value, overwriting the receiver. That surprise is the most common bidirectional bug.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty a = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty("A");
javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty b = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty("B");
a.bindBidirectional(b);
System.out.println(a.get() + " " + b.get());   // B B: the argument's value wins

cards.front: Which property API converts a double property to a formatted String for display?
cards.extra: Fluent API methods like Bindings.format or DoubleBinding.asString("%.1f") let a String-typed property such as text mirror a numeric one, with the number formatted to one decimal place.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.DoubleProperty price = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty(12.5);
javafx.beans.binding.StringBinding formatted = price.asString("%.1f");
javafx.beans.property.StringProperty display = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty();
display.bind(formatted);   // the numeric binding formats the double as a String
System.out.println(display.get());   // 12.5

cards.front: What three roles does a change listener's callback receive?
cards.extra: Because change listeners are generic, the value parameters arrive correctly typed and need no cast — unlike the invalidation listener's raw Observable.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty count = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty(0);
javafx.beans.value.ChangeListener<Number> listener = (observable, oldValue, newValue) -> {
    System.out.println(observable + " " + oldValue + " " + newValue);   // all three roles
};
count.addListener(listener);
count.set(1);   // observable, 0, 1

cards.front: What JavaFX mechanism links a property's value to one or more other properties without writing a listener?
cards.extra: Bindings express 'this value is derived from those values' declaratively, so updates propagate automatically. When types differ or a computation is needed, the fluent/bindings APIs build the expression.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty total = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty(0);
javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty count = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty(2);
total.bind(count.multiply(10));   // binding links values without writing a listener
count.set(3);
System.out.println(total.get());   // 30

cards.front: Which observer is used to trigger logic when a Transition stops running?
cards.extra: The status property is read-only and swings between RUNNING, PAUSED and STOPPED; a change listener can react to each transition, e.g. recoloring a label by state.
cards.example:
javafx.animation.FadeTransition fade = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1));
fade.statusProperty().addListener((o, oldV, newV) -> {
  if (newV == javafx.animation.Animation.Status.STOPPED) System.out.println("transition stopped");
});
fade.play();

cards.front: Why prefer a layout pane over placing nodes at fixed coordinates?
cards.back: The pane re-arranges on resize; coordinates don't
cards.extra: Coordinates stay where you put them, so resizing clips or uncenters content unless you write resize-handling code. A layout control responds to resizing, insertion/removal, and children changing size.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.VBox pane = new javafx.scene.layout.VBox(8);
pane.getChildren().addAll(new javafx.scene.control.Label("a"), new javafx.scene.control.Label("b"));
pane.resize(300, 200);   // the layout pane re-arranges its children on resize
javafx.scene.layout.Pane fixed = new javafx.scene.layout.Pane();
javafx.scene.control.Label lone = new javafx.scene.control.Label("stays put");
lone.relocate(10, 10);   // fixed coordinates do not re-arrange

cards.front: Which two ObservableList methods add children to a layout pane's getChildren()?
cards.extra: Some panes also expose specialised add helpers (GridPane by row/column, BorderPane by region), but every pane's children list accepts add/addAll directly.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.VBox box = new javafx.scene.layout.VBox();
javafx.collections.ObservableList<javafx.scene.Node> kids = box.getChildren();
kids.add(new javafx.scene.control.Label("one"));
kids.addAll(new javafx.scene.control.Label("two"), new javafx.scene.control.Label("three"));
System.out.println(kids.size());   // add() and addAll() add children

cards.front: StackPane children are added ellipse-then-text. Which is on top?
cards.back: The text — later children render in front
cards.extra: StackPane stacks from back to front in insertion order, so adding the shape first keeps it behind and visible; reversing the order would let the ellipse hide the text.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.StackPane stack = new javafx.scene.layout.StackPane();
javafx.scene.shape.Ellipse ellipse = new javafx.scene.shape.Ellipse(50, 30);
javafx.scene.text.Text text = new javafx.scene.text.Text("label");
stack.getChildren().addAll(ellipse, text);
System.out.println(stack.getChildren().indexOf(text) > stack.getChildren().indexOf(ellipse));   // true: text is on top

cards.front: In a StackPane, per-node alignment vs pane-wide alignment?
cards.extra: Overriding one child's alignment leaves siblings where the pane default puts them, e.g. a bottom-anchored label over a still-centered shape.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.StackPane pane = new javafx.scene.layout.StackPane();
javafx.scene.text.Text text = new javafx.scene.text.Text("bottom");
javafx.scene.layout.StackPane.setAlignment(text, javafx.geometry.Pos.BOTTOM);   // per-node alignment
pane.setAlignment(javafx.geometry.Pos.CENTER);   // pane-wide alignment
pane.getChildren().add(text);

cards.front: In BorderPane, what does setMargin(node, insets) do?
cards.back: Adds space around one node inside its region
cards.extra: Insets are given as top, right, bottom, left. Margins are the counterpart to the pane's own padding and apply to any layout pane via the same static method.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.BorderPane pane = new javafx.scene.layout.BorderPane();
javafx.scene.control.Label top = new javafx.scene.control.Label("Top");
pane.setTop(top);
javafx.scene.layout.BorderPane.setMargin(top, new javafx.geometry.Insets(10, 20, 10, 20));   // top/right/bottom/left
System.out.println(javafx.scene.layout.BorderPane.getMargin(top));   // space around this one child in its region

cards.front: What does SplitPane divide its space into?
cards.back: Resizable areas split by a draggable divider
cards.extra: Orientation is horizontal or vertical; each area typically hosts another layout pane. Users drag the divider to rebalance the areas at runtime.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.SplitPane split = new javafx.scene.control.SplitPane();
split.getItems().addAll(new javafx.scene.control.Label("left"), new javafx.scene.control.Label("right"));
// two resizable areas separated by a draggable divider
System.out.println(split.getItems().size());   // 2

cards.front: Which layout pane gives a fixed single-direction row or column of children?
cards.extra: Nesting one inside the other yields a grid-like structure without GridPane's cell model — a VBox of HBoxes is a common form layout.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.HBox row = new javafx.scene.layout.HBox(8);
row.getChildren().addAll(new javafx.scene.control.Button("A"), new javafx.scene.control.Button("B"));   // row
javafx.scene.layout.VBox column = new javafx.scene.layout.VBox(8);
column.getChildren().addAll(new javafx.scene.control.Label("A"), new javafx.scene.control.Label("B"));   // column
System.out.println(row.getOrientation() + " / " + column.getOrientation());

cards.front: What does a linear gradient Stop consist of?
cards.extra: The offset positions the color along the gradient axis. JavaFX interpolates proportionally between neighbouring stops, which is how a three-stop blue→lightblue→green wash is built.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.paint.Stop red = new javafx.scene.paint.Stop(0.0, javafx.scene.paint.Color.RED);
javafx.scene.paint.Stop blue = new javafx.scene.paint.Stop(1.0, javafx.scene.paint.Color.BLUE);
javafx.scene.paint.LinearGradient g = new javafx.scene.paint.LinearGradient(0, 0, 1, 0, true, javafx.scene.paint.CycleMethod.NO_CYCLE, red, blue);
System.out.println(red.getOffset() + " " + red.getColor() + " -> " + blue.getOffset() + " " + blue.getColor());

cards.front: new LinearGradient(...) takes an x-range then a y-range. Which combination makes a vertical gradient?
cards.extra: Varying x with constant y gives a horizontal gradient; varying both gives a diagonal one. Reversing either range flips the color order.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.paint.Stop a = new javafx.scene.paint.Stop(0, javafx.scene.paint.Color.RED);
javafx.scene.paint.Stop b = new javafx.scene.paint.Stop(1, javafx.scene.paint.Color.BLUE);
javafx.scene.paint.LinearGradient vertical = new javafx.scene.paint.LinearGradient(0, 0, 0, 1, true, javafx.scene.paint.CycleMethod.NO_CYCLE, a, b);
System.out.println(vertical.getStartX() + "," + vertical.getStartY() + " -> " + vertical.getEndX() + "," + vertical.getEndY());   // x constant, y varies

cards.front: The proportional boolean of a gradient — what does true mean?
cards.back: Gradient coordinates are relative to the shape (0..1)
cards.extra: With true, 0 and 1 map to the shape's own edges, so the gradient stretches to fit. With false, the values are absolute in the parent's local coordinate system.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle box = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(40, 40);
javafx.scene.paint.LinearGradient g = new javafx.scene.paint.LinearGradient(
    0, 0, 1, 1, true, javafx.scene.paint.CycleMethod.NO_CYCLE,
    new javafx.scene.paint.Stop(0, javafx.scene.paint.Color.RED),
    new javafx.scene.paint.Stop(1, javafx.scene.paint.Color.BLUE));   // true: 0..1 relative to the shape
box.setFill(g);

cards.front: What does the CycleMethod of a gradient control?
cards.extra: NO_CYCLE paints the stop pattern once and clamps beyond it. REFLECT and REPEAT tile it, which is why CycleMethod sits beside the proportional flag in the constructor.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.paint.Stop[] stops = { new javafx.scene.paint.Stop(0, javafx.scene.paint.Color.RED), new javafx.scene.paint.Stop(1, javafx.scene.paint.Color.BLUE) };
for (javafx.scene.paint.CycleMethod cm : javafx.scene.paint.CycleMethod.values()) {
  javafx.scene.paint.LinearGradient g = new javafx.scene.paint.LinearGradient(0, 0, 1, 0, true, cm, stops);
  System.out.println(cm);   // NO_CYCLE, REFLECT, REPEAT: whether the pattern repeats
}

cards.front: What parameters define a DropShadow, and what do the x/y offsets simulate?
cards.back: Color, radius, and x/y offsets — simulating a light source direction
cards.extra: Offsets place the shadow relative to the shape's outer edge. Positive x and y shift it right and down, i.e. light from the upper left; zero offsets wrap the shadow evenly around the shape.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle box = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(40, 40);
javafx.scene.effect.DropShadow shadow = new javafx.scene.effect.DropShadow(javafx.scene.paint.Color.DARKGRAY, 10, 4, 4);
box.setEffect(shadow);   // color, radius, offsetX, offsetY: shadow down-right implies light upper-left
System.out.println(shadow.getOffsetX() + " " + shadow.getOffsetY());

cards.front: What does a Reflection effect do, and what is its fraction?
cards.back: Mirrors the child downward, fading out; fraction = reflect height share
cards.extra: A fraction of 0.8 reflects eight-tenths of the component's height. Top and bottom opacity set the fade, and the offset sets how many pixels below the shape the mirror starts.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.text.Text text = new javafx.scene.text.Text("MyShapes");
javafx.scene.effect.Reflection reflection = new javafx.scene.effect.Reflection();
reflection.setFraction(0.8);   // eight-tenths of the component height is reflected below it
text.setEffect(reflection);    // mirrored downward and faded to transparent

cards.front: A click handler is attached to the front Text of a StackPane. The user clicks the ellipse behind it — does the handler fire?
cards.back: No — they are sibling leaf nodes, not nested
cards.extra: Though they visually overlap, the ellipse is not a child of the text, so events don't bubble through it. Attach handlers to both, or once to the StackPane to catch any click inside.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.StackPane stack = new javafx.scene.layout.StackPane();
javafx.scene.shape.Ellipse ellipse = new javafx.scene.shape.Ellipse(50, 30);
javafx.scene.text.Text front = new javafx.scene.text.Text("front");
front.setOnMouseClicked(e -> System.out.println("clicked front"));
stack.getChildren().addAll(ellipse, front);   // sibling leaf nodes: clicking the ellipse behind does not fire it
System.out.println(stack.getChildren().size());   // 2

cards.front: ParallelTransition vs SequentialTransition?
cards.back: Parallel runs animations at once; Sequential one after another
cards.extra: Sequential chains each child's end to the next one's start, so total time is the sum. Parallel overlaps them, so total time is the longest child's duration.
cards.example:
javafx.animation.FadeTransition a = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1));
javafx.animation.FillTransition b = new javafx.animation.FillTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1));
new javafx.animation.ParallelTransition(a, b).play();     // both at once
new javafx.animation.SequentialTransition(a, b).play();   // one after another

cards.front: play() vs playFromStart() on a paused transition?
cards.back: play() resumes from current time; playFromStart() restarts at 0
cards.extra: That distinction makes a pause/resume toggle work: pause() then play() continues where it stopped, whereas playFromStart() jumps back to the beginning.
cards.example:
javafx.animation.FadeTransition fade = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(2));
fade.play(); fade.pause();   // paused partway through
fade.play();                 // resumes from the current time
fade.playFromStart();        // restarts at time 0

cards.front: What are the three values of Animation.Status?
cards.extra: getStatus() returns them, and the read-only status property fires change events as the animation crosses between them — handy for driving UI state.
cards.example:
for (javafx.animation.Animation.Status s : javafx.animation.Animation.Status.values()) System.out.println(s);   // RUNNING, PAUSED, STOPPED
javafx.animation.FadeTransition fade = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1));
System.out.println(fade.getStatus());   // STOPPED before play()

cards.front: What does autoReverse do to a transition?
cards.back: Plays the animation backwards on alternating cycles
cards.extra: Combined with cycleCount it produces a there-and-back-again loop: cycle 1 forward, cycle 2 in reverse, and so on, instead of snapping back to the start.
cards.example:
javafx.animation.FadeTransition fade = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1));
fade.setAutoReverse(true);
fade.setCycleCount(2);   // alternates: forward, then backward on the next cycle
fade.play();

cards.front: What does RotateTransition modify on a node, and in what unit?
cards.extra: A 0→360 rotation over 2500 ms is one full turn. Because the property lives on the node, it affects the node's children and its effects too.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.Node node = new javafx.scene.control.Label("spin");
javafx.animation.RotateTransition spin = new javafx.animation.RotateTransition(javafx.util.Duration.millis(2500), node);
spin.setFromAngle(0); spin.setToAngle(360);   // degrees: one full turn of the rotate property
spin.play();

cards.front: Applying a transition to a parent StackPane — what else moves besides its children?
cards.back: Everything drawn with the node, including its effects
cards.extra: Effects such as drop shadow and reflection are rendered as part of that node, so rotating or translating the parent carries them along, which keeps the visual coherent.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.StackPane pane = new javafx.scene.layout.StackPane();
pane.setEffect(new javafx.scene.effect.DropShadow());   // the effect belongs to the parent node
pane.getChildren().add(new javafx.scene.control.Label("child"));
javafx.animation.RotateTransition spin = new javafx.animation.RotateTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1), pane);
spin.play();   // children and the parent's effect rotate together

cards.front: Which JavaFX class schedules per-frame work and is the lowest-level animation tool?
cards.extra: Its handle(long now) runs once per frame on the JavaFX Application Thread, giving frame-accurate control that transitions and timelines do not. Remember to call stop() to end it.
cards.example:
javafx.animation.AnimationTimer timer = new javafx.animation.AnimationTimer() {
    public void handle(long now) { System.out.println("frame at " + now + " ns"); }
};
timer.start();   // handle(long) is called each frame: lowest-level animation tool

cards.front: What is FXML?
cards.back: An XML markup language for declaring JavaFX scene graphs
cards.extra: Instead of building nodes in Java, you describe the hierarchy declaratively, which mirrors the scene graph's own tree and keeps view code separate from behaviour.
cards.example:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<?import javafx.scene.control.*?>
<VBox xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml" spacing="8">   <!-- XML markup declaring the scene graph -->
  <Label text="Hello" />
  <Button text="OK" />
</VBox>

cards.front: Which class parses an FXML file and builds the scene graph?
cards.extra: The loader instantiates the elements, wires attributes and events, and returns the root node, which the application then wraps in a Scene. Each FXML file is usually paired with one controller class.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static void m() throws Exception {
    javafx.fxml.FXMLLoader loader = new javafx.fxml.FXMLLoader(Ex.class.getResource("view.fxml"));
    javafx.scene.Parent root = loader.load();   // parses the FXML file and builds the scene graph
  }
}

cards.front: Which FXML attribute names the controller class for a view?
cards.extra: It is set on the top-level (root) element. The loader instantiates that class and injects fields or event handlers marked with @FXML.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static void m() throws Exception {
    javafx.fxml.FXMLLoader loader = new javafx.fxml.FXMLLoader(Ex.class.getResource("view.fxml"));
    System.out.println(loader.load().getController().getClass().getSimpleName());   // FXML: fx:controller="com.example.MyController" names this class
  }
}

cards.front: How does a controller class access a node declared in FXML?
cards.back: A field annotated @FXML with the name from fx:id
cards.extra: The name must match exactly; a typo leaves the field null at runtime with no compile error. The loader performs the injection after constructing the controller.
cards.example:
class PersonController {
    @javafx.fxml.FXML private javafx.scene.control.TextField firstName;   // field name equals fx:id
}
// FXML declares <TextField fx:id="firstName" />; the loader injects it after constructing the controller

cards.front: How does an FXML attribute point an event at a controller method?
cards.extra: For example onMouseClicked="#handleMouseClick". The method must be accessible to the loader and annotated @FXML; the leading # marks it as a controller method reference.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static void m() throws Exception {
    javafx.fxml.FXMLLoader loader = new javafx.fxml.FXMLLoader(Ex.class.getResource("view.fxml"));
    System.out.println("onMouseClicked=\"#handleClick\" -> " + loader.load().getController().getClass().getSimpleName());
  }
}

cards.front: Which interface lets a controller run setup code after FXML injection?
cards.extra: The loader calls initialize() once the @FXML fields are populated, making it the right place for bindings, listeners, and configuring objects the FXML did not create.
cards.example:
class DemoController implements javafx.fxml.Initializable {
  public void initialize(java.net.URL url, java.util.ResourceBundle rb) { System.out.println("FXML injection done"); }
}
// FXMLLoader calls initialize() after injecting fields annotated with @FXML

cards.front: What is the one @FXML node that is not required to have an fx:id?
cards.extra: Leave fx:id off children the controller doesn't touch — for example decorative shapes inside a pane. Only nodes referenced in Java need the attribute.
cards.example:
class PersonController {
    @javafx.fxml.FXML private javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle badge;   // fx:id="badge": controller reads it
}
// Decorative Rectangle has no fx:id: the controller never accesses it, so no field is needed
// FXML: <Rectangle ... /> versus <Rectangle fx:id="badge" ... />

cards.front: What is the name of the default JavaFX stylesheet?
cards.extra: It ships inside the platform's runtime JAR and supplies the default look. Custom stylesheets can be added to the scene's stylesheets list to augment or override it.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.StackPane root = new javafx.scene.layout.StackPane();
javafx.scene.Scene scene = new javafx.scene.Scene(root, 400, 300);
System.out.println("default stylesheet: modena.css");   // ships with the platform
scene.getStylesheets().add("custom.css");   // add stylesheets to augment or override Modena

cards.front: Which Scene list accepts stylesheets at runtime?
cards.extra: Adding a file URL there applies its style classes to the whole scene. You then call getStyleClass().add(...) on individual nodes to attach a class.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.Scene scene = new javafx.scene.Scene(new javafx.scene.layout.StackPane(), 300, 200);
scene.getStylesheets().add("Styles.css");   // the Scene's runtime stylesheet list
System.out.println(scene.getStylesheets());

cards.front: Which node method applies a CSS style class defined in a stylesheet?
cards.extra: The class name must match the selector in the CSS without the dot. Multiple classes can be attached, and the most specific selector wins, much like the web.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.Button button = new javafx.scene.control.Button("Save");
button.getStyleClass().add("primary-action");   // matches .primary-action in the stylesheet
System.out.println(button.getStyleClass());

cards.front: Declaring the stylesheet in FXML rather than in start() — what is the benefit?
cards.extra: Loading the CSS from the FXML file makes the designer render with those styles, so the visual preview matches the running app instead of showing unstyled defaults.
cards.example:
<AnchorPane xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml" fx:controller="demo.PersonController">
  <stylesheets>
    <URL value="@person.css" />   <!-- declared in FXML so Scene Builder previews the styles -->
  </stylesheets>
  <Label text="Name" />
</AnchorPane>

cards.front: What kind of tool is Scene Builder?
cards.extra: It renders the scene visually and generates FXML, with an inspector for properties, layout and event handlers. It started at Oracle and is now open source, distributed by Gluon.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static void m() throws Exception {
    javafx.fxml.FXMLLoader loader = new javafx.fxml.FXMLLoader(Ex.class.getResource("designed.fxml"));   // Scene Builder's drag-and-drop FXML
    System.out.println(loader.load());   // stand-alone UI designer output as a scene graph
  }
}

cards.front: What architectural pattern does separating FXML (view) from a controller class promote?
cards.extra: FXML holds structure, the controller holds behaviour, and the model holds data and business logic — which keeps larger interfaces maintainable and testable.
cards.example:
record Person(String name) {}                       // Model: data
class PersonController {                            // Controller: behaviour
    @javafx.fxml.FXML private javafx.scene.control.TextField name;
}
// View: person.fxml declares the scene graph; FXMLLoader wires view and controller (MVC)

cards.front: How does a JavaFX release relate to a JDK release version-wise?
cards.extra: JavaFX is a standalone component layered on the JDK, so pick a JDK the chosen JavaFX version supports. Newer JavaFX releases set a minimum JDK — e.g. JavaFX 26 needs JDK 24+.
cards.example:
System.out.println(System.getProperty("java.version"));   // JDK 21 -> pair with JavaFX 21 (same major version)
System.out.println("JavaFX 26 needs JDK 24+");            // a newer JavaFX release can require a higher JDK

cards.front: How is JavaFX distributed — is it part of the JDK?
cards.back: No — it's a standalone SDK with jmod files
cards.extra: Since Oracle removed it from the JDK, you download a JavaFX SDK archive (or jmods) separately and point the launcher at it. Licensing is GPL v2 with the Classpath Exception.
cards.example:
# JavaFX is standalone: an SDK or a jmod archive downloaded separately from the JDK
javac --module-path /path/to/javafx-sdk/lib --add-modules javafx.controls HelloWorldFX.java
jlink --module-path /path/to/javafx-jmods --add-modules javafx.controls --output myjre

cards.front: Which JavaFX module must be added to compile a basic Controls application?
cards.extra: It transitively pulls in javafx.graphics, so listing controls alone resolves the graphics dependency. Add it to both the javac and java invocations via --module-path and --add-modules.
cards.example:
module myapp {
    requires javafx.controls;   // add this module to compile a basic Controls application
}

cards.front: Which additional module do you need when the UI uses FXML?
cards.extra: Add it to both the compile and run command lines alongside javafx.controls. Without it the loader class is missing at runtime, not at compile time in every case.
cards.example:
module myapp {
    requires javafx.controls;
    requires javafx.fxml;   // the additional module when the UI uses FXML
}

cards.front: What do the jmod files in a JavaFX archive let you do with jlink?
cards.back: Build a custom runtime image bundling JavaFX
cards.extra: Use the jmods on the jlink module path to link a trimmed JDK that already contains the JavaFX modules (and optionally your app). Your project must then be modular, with module-info.java requiring them.
cards.example:
jlink --module-path "$JAVAFX_JMODS:$JAVA_HOME/jmods" --add-modules javafx.controls,javafx.fxml --output my-runtime
# jmod files on the module path let jlink bundle JavaFX into a custom runtime image
my-runtime/bin/java -m myapp/com.example.Main

cards.front: Since JDK 24 (JEP 472), what must JavaFX apps do about native access?
cards.extra: Three JavaFX modules (javafx.graphics, media, web) load native libraries. Relying on the default is deprecated and emits warnings; --enable-native-access makes the intent explicit and future-proofs the run.
cards.example:
java --enable-native-access=javafx.graphics,javafx.media,javafx.web -m myapp/com.example.Main
# Since JDK 24 (JEP 472), JavaFX's native libraries need native access enabled explicitly at startup

cards.front: What interface does the JavaFX animation framework manipulate values through?
cards.extra: A WritableValue is anything with a readable, settable value. Because node properties implement it, animations can drive width, opacity, translateX and similar properties uniformly.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.value.WritableValue<Number> w = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty(1.0);
w.setValue(2.0);   // the animation framework reads and writes through WritableValue<T>
System.out.println(w.getValue());   // 2.0

cards.front: Can Animation be extended directly?
cards.extra: Animation is abstract and holds shared machinery: rate, cycleCount, delay, status and the play/pause/stop controls. Its two concrete families cover preset effects and free-form keyframes.
cards.example:
class MyTransition extends javafx.animation.Transition {
    @Override protected void interpolate(double frac) { System.out.println(frac); }
}
class MyTimeline extends javafx.animation.Timeline { }   // Animation is abstract: extend these, not it

cards.front: What does an Animation's rate property control?
cards.extra: A rate of 2 plays twice as fast, 0.5 at half speed, and a negative rate plays backwards. It pairs with targetFramerate, which caps how many frames per second are rendered.
cards.example:
javafx.animation.Timeline timeline = new javafx.animation.Timeline();
timeline.setRate(2.0);   // double speed
timeline.setRate(-1.0);  // reverse direction
System.out.println(timeline.getRate());

cards.front: What is the relationship between cycleDuration and totalDuration?
cards.extra: cycleDuration is one pass from start to end at rate 1.0. totalDuration includes the repeats, or is Duration.INDEFINITE for a looping animation.
cards.example:
double cycleDuration = 2.0;
int cycleCount = 3;
double totalDuration = cycleDuration * cycleCount;
System.out.println(totalDuration);   // 6.0: totalDuration = cycleDuration x cycleCount

cards.front: Which property must be positive and cannot change while an animation runs?
cards.extra: Changing the repeat count mid-run has no defined meaning, so the framework forbids it. Stop the animation and set it, then play again.
cards.example:
javafx.animation.FadeTransition fade = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1));
fade.setCycleCount(3);   // positive and fixed while the animation runs
fade.play();
System.out.println(fade.getCycleCount());

cards.front: Which transition animates opacity, and what does it interpolate?
cards.extra: It steps opacity from 1 (opaque) to 0 (transparent) over the duration, at each frame. Fading out to 0 and back in is the standard way to reveal UI.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.Node node = new javafx.scene.control.Label("fade");
javafx.animation.FadeTransition fade = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1), node);
fade.setFromValue(1.0); fade.setToValue(0.0);   // interpolates the node's opacity property
fade.play();

cards.front: Which transition changes a shape's fill color over time?
cards.extra: Use StrokeTransition for the outline instead. Both operate on Shape, whereas the generic node transitions work on any Node.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle rect = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(20, 20, javafx.scene.paint.Color.RED);
javafx.animation.FillTransition fill = new javafx.animation.FillTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1), rect, javafx.scene.paint.Color.BLUE);
fill.play();   // updates the Shape's fill property over time

cards.front: Which transition moves a node along a predefined path built from shapes?
cards.extra: It updates translateX/translateY along the path, and can also rotate the node when orientation is set to ORTHOGONAL_TO_TANGENT so the node turns with the curve.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.shape.Path path = new javafx.scene.shape.Path();
path.getElements().addAll(new javafx.scene.shape.MoveTo(0, 0), new javafx.scene.shape.LineTo(200, 0));
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle node = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(10, 10);
javafx.animation.PathTransition pt = new javafx.animation.PathTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(2), path, node);
pt.play();   // node moves along a predefined path built from shapes

cards.front: Which transition animates scaleX, scaleY, scaleZ?
cards.extra: Scaling above 1.0 enlarges and below 1.0 shrinks, pivoting around the node's center unless the pivot is changed. Pair it with rotate for a pop effect.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle box = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(40, 40);
javafx.animation.ScaleTransition scale = new javafx.animation.ScaleTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1), box);
scale.setToX(2); scale.setToY(2); scale.setToZ(2);   // animates scaleX, scaleY, scaleZ
scale.play();

cards.front: In a SequentialTransition, what does an INDEFINITE child do?
cards.back: Blocks every later animation in the sequence
cards.extra: The sequence never reaches the next child, so any following step silently never runs. Only the final child may be indefinite.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.Node node = new javafx.scene.control.Label("x");
javafx.animation.FadeTransition fade = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.millis(300), node);
fade.setCycleCount(javafx.animation.Animation.INDEFINITE);
javafx.animation.PauseTransition later = new javafx.animation.PauseTransition(javafx.util.Duration.millis(100));
javafx.animation.SequentialTransition seq = new javafx.animation.SequentialTransition(fade, later);
seq.play();   // INDEFINITE child never ends: every later animation is blocked

cards.front: What is a PauseTransition used for?
cards.extra: It occupies time in a sequential chain so a later animation starts after a wait. A child transition with no node of its own inherits its parent's node.
cards.example:
javafx.animation.PauseTransition pause = new javafx.animation.PauseTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1));
javafx.animation.SequentialTransition seq = new javafx.animation.SequentialTransition(pause);
seq.play();   // a delay with no property change, useful inside a sequence
System.out.println(pause.getDuration());

cards.front: When you set a Node on a SequentialTransition, what happens to children without one?
cards.extra: That means you can build a multi-step animation over one node and set its node only once, on the parent transition.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.StackPane root = new javafx.scene.layout.StackPane();
javafx.animation.FadeTransition fade = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1));
javafx.animation.PauseTransition pause = new javafx.animation.PauseTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1));
javafx.animation.SequentialTransition seq = new javafx.animation.SequentialTransition(fade, pause);
seq.setNode(root);   // children without a node implicitly use the parent's node

cards.front: What does a Timeline hold, and why choose it over transitions?
cards.back: A series of KeyFrames over any WritableValue
cards.extra: Use a Timeline when no built-in transition targets the properties you need, or when the animation does not follow a simple from-to shape. It offers more control at the cost of more verbosity.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty x = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty(0);
javafx.animation.KeyFrame kf = new javafx.animation.KeyFrame(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1), new javafx.animation.KeyValue(x, 200.0));
javafx.animation.Timeline timeline = new javafx.animation.Timeline(kf);   // KeyFrames over any WritableValue<T>
timeline.play();

cards.front: What memory risk does an infinite Timeline create?
cards.extra: The FX runtime holds a reference to a running Timeline, so an indefinite one keeps its targets alive. Call stop() when the animation is no longer needed.
cards.example:
javafx.animation.Timeline infinite = new javafx.animation.Timeline();
infinite.setCycleCount(javafx.animation.Animation.INDEFINITE);
infinite.play();
// the FX runtime keeps referencing animated objects, so they are never garbage collected
infinite.stop();

cards.front: What does a KeyFrame contain?
cards.back: A time (cue point) and a set of KeyValues
cards.extra: Each KeyValue maps one WritableValue to its target value at that moment. A named KeyFrame can be jumped to with playFrom(name) and can run an onFinished handler.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty x = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty(0);
javafx.animation.KeyValue kv = new javafx.animation.KeyValue(x, 200.0);
javafx.animation.KeyFrame frame = new javafx.animation.KeyFrame(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1), kv);   // cue point + KeyValues
javafx.animation.Timeline timeline = new javafx.animation.Timeline(frame);

cards.front: What does a KeyValue bind together?
cards.back: One WritableValue<T> and its target value of type T
cards.extra: An optional Interpolator sets the rate of change for that value. KeyValue instances are immutable, so you create a new one to change the target.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty text = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty("old");
javafx.animation.KeyValue kv = new javafx.animation.KeyValue(text, "new");
System.out.println(kv.getTarget() + " -> " + kv.getEndValue());   // WritableValue<T> and target value T

cards.front: Interpolator.LINEAR vs DISCRETE — how do they differ?
cards.extra: Discrete holds each value until the next one and then snaps, with no intermediate frames. Linear moves at an unchanging pace across the whole interval.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty x = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleDoubleProperty(0);
javafx.animation.KeyValue linear = new javafx.animation.KeyValue(x, 10, javafx.animation.Interpolator.LINEAR);
javafx.animation.KeyValue discrete = new javafx.animation.KeyValue(x, 10, javafx.animation.Interpolator.DISCRETE);
// LINEAR changes at a constant rate; DISCRETE jumps straight to the end value

cards.front: Which interpolator do JavaFX transitions use by default?
cards.extra: It starts slowly, speeds up in the middle and slows at the end. The exception is ParallelTransition and SequentialTransition, which have no single interpolation of their own.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.Node node = new javafx.scene.control.Label("x");
javafx.animation.FadeTransition fade = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1), node);
System.out.println(fade.getInterpolator() == javafx.animation.Interpolator.EASE_BOTH);   // true by default
fade.setInterpolator(javafx.animation.Interpolator.EASE_BOTH);   // starts slow, fast in the middle, slow at end

cards.front: What is the signature of AnimationTimer's per-frame method, and in what unit is now?
cards.extra: It is called every frame while active, and all AnimationTimers invoked in that frame receive the same timestamp. start() and stop() manage its lifetime.
cards.example:
javafx.animation.AnimationTimer timer = new javafx.animation.AnimationTimer() {
  public void handle(long now) { System.out.println("frame at " + now + " ns"); }
};
timer.start();   // now is the frame timestamp in nanoseconds

cards.front: To sustain 30 fps, how much time can a JavaFX frame take in total?
cards.extra: 1000 ms ÷ 30 ≈ 33.3 ms. The handle() method runs on the JavaFX Application Thread, so blocking or heavy work there directly causes dropped frames.
cards.example:
double fps = 30.0;
double millisPerFrame = 1000.0 / fps;
System.out.println(millisPerFrame);   // about 33 ms total per frame at 30 fps

cards.front: In JavaFX, which property tells assistive technology what kind of control a node is?
cards.extra: It is an enumeration property on Node. Built-in controls such as Button and TextField already set theirs; only custom elements need you to assign one explicitly.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleRole;
import javafx.scene.control.Button;
Button b = new Button();
AccessibleRole role = b.getAccessibleRole(); // an AccessibleRole enum constant

cards.front: Which JavaFX controls need no manual accessibleRole?
cards.extra: The platform already declares their roles, so overriding is only for refinement. Custom nodes must choose the closest matching AccessibleRole or screen readers see nothing meaningful.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.Button button = new javafx.scene.control.Button("OK");
javafx.scene.control.TextField field = new javafx.scene.control.TextField();
javafx.scene.control.Slider slider = new javafx.scene.control.Slider();
System.out.println(button.getAccessibleRole() + " " + field.getAccessibleRole() + " " + slider.getAccessibleRole());
// built-in controls already declare roles: no manual setAccessibleRole needed

cards.front: Why does accessibleRoleDescription exist if roles already carry meaning?
cards.back: The enum has no user-defined roles — this refines one
cards.extra: You keep a valid standard role but describe it more precisely. Leave it null (the built-in default) and the screen reader announces the platform's native description.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.Node;
Node seat = new javafx.scene.control.Button();
seat.setAccessibleRole(javafx.scene.AccessibleRole.BUTTON);
seat.setAccessibleRoleDescription("Seat reservation toggle"); // no user-defined roles in the enum

cards.front: Which Node property specifies the text a screen reader speaks as the node's content?
cards.extra: It defaults to null on built-in controls, which then derive their spoken content from the control (a button's label). Set it to say something the visual label cannot, like a field's expected format.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.Node;
Node field = new javafx.scene.control.TextField();
field.setAccessibleText("Enter your name"); // what the screen reader speaks as content

cards.front: Which Node property supplies a longer explanation of how a control works?
cards.extra: Use it when the label alone is ambiguous. If it is unset and the node has a tooltip, the tooltip text is handed to the screen reader as the help instead.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.control.Slider;
Slider opacity = new Slider();
opacity.setAccessibleHelp("Drag to change preview opacity from 0 to 100 percent");

cards.front: accessibleHelp is null and the node has a tooltip — what does the screen reader receive?
cards.extra: That fallback means an existing tooltip silently doubles as accessibility help, which is convenient but can leak inappropriate phrasing into the spoken help.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.control.Button;
Button save = new Button("Save");
save.setTooltip(new javafx.scene.control.Tooltip("Save the form"));
save.setAccessibleHelp(null); // screen reader falls back to the tooltip text

cards.front: What does Label.labelFor connect?
cards.back: A label to the control it describes
cards.extra: Setting it makes the screen reader announce the label text together with the control, which is how form fields become self-describing. Default is null.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.control.Label;
import javafx.scene.control.TextField;
TextField name = new TextField();
Label label = new Label("Name:");
label.setLabelFor(name);

cards.front: How does JavaFX store accessibility information?
cards.back: In the scene graph itself, no shadow tree
cards.extra: There is no parallel accessibility hierarchy to keep in sync, so CSS and FXML can describe accessible properties like any other. That avoids duplicated data and stale copies.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.Scene;
import javafx.scene.control.Button;
Scene scene = new Scene(new Button("Save"));
scene.getRoot().setAccessibleText("Save button"); // metadata on the node, no shadow tree

cards.front: When does JavaFX activate its accessibility machinery?
cards.back: Only when a screen reader is active
cards.extra: Keeping the mechanism dormant otherwise holds runtime overhead low. Apps can observe activation through Platform.accessibilityActiveProperty.
cards.example:
import javafx.application.Platform;
boolean active = Platform.isAccessibilityActive(); // false until a screen reader is active

cards.front: What is software accessibility?
cards.back: Design so software is usable with disabilities
cards.extra: It covers visual, auditory, motor and cognitive needs — screen readers, keyboard-only use, high contrast, zoom. The platform exposes semantics; the application must supply the meaning.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.control.Button;
Button save = new Button("Save");
save.setAccessibleHelp("Ctrl+S also saves"); // operable without a pointer

cards.front: Where should accessibility metadata for a form be attached in an FXML/CSS/controller app?
cards.extra: The controller already owns interaction, so keeping accessibleText, accessibleHelp and tooltips there keeps visual and non-visual guidance aligned as the UI evolves.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.control.TextField;
class AccessibleFxController {
    TextField name = new TextField();
    void configure() { name.setAccessibleHelp("Enter your full name"); } // metadata beside behaviour
}

cards.front: Tooltip vs accessibleHelp — who each is for?
cards.extra: A tooltip shows on hover and is mouse-centric; accessibleHelp is spoken context for assistive tech. Providing both near each other keeps them from contradicting each other.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.control.Button;
Button save = new Button("Save");
save.setTooltip(new javafx.scene.control.Tooltip("Save - pointer users"));
save.setAccessibleHelp("Saves the form - screen readers");

cards.front: A custom Rectangle acting as a preview slider indicator — what is it to a screen reader?
cards.extra: Sighteds infer meaning from context; the reader gets nothing. Assign a role, a role description, accessible text and accessible help so the shape carries the same meaning.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle marker = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(8, 8, javafx.scene.paint.Color.BLUE);
System.out.println(marker.getAccessibleRole());   // a plain shape carries no meaning for a screen reader
marker.setAccessibleRole(javafx.scene.AccessibleRole.SLIDER);
marker.setAccessibleText("Volume 40 percent");   // semantics supplied explicitly

cards.front: What does setFocusTraversable(true) do for a custom node?
cards.back: Puts it in the Tab traversal order
cards.extra: Without it, keyboard users cannot reach the node at all, even if it handles keys. Also needs a key handler, because custom nodes do not inherit control behaviour.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle;
class Preview {
    Rectangle node = new Rectangle();
    Preview() { node.setFocusTraversable(true); } // joins Tab traversal order
}

cards.front: Why split normal and high-contrast styling into two stylesheets?
cards.back: Themes switch by swapping stylesheets at runtime
cards.extra: The controller reacts to the checkbox by adding or removing high-contrast.css; it never knows color values. CSS remains the single source of truth for appearance.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.Scene;
class Themes {
    Scene scene;
    void toggle(boolean contrast) { scene.getStylesheets().setAll(contrast ? "high-contrast.css" : "base.css"); }
}

cards.front: In module-info.java, which directive lets the FXML loader reach controller fields?
cards.extra: FXML injects @FXML fields and calls handler methods reflectively, so the package must be open to javafx.fxml specifically. Without it loading fails at runtime.
cards.example:
module a11y.app {
    requires javafx.fxml;
    opens com.example.a11y to javafx.fxml;
}

cards.front: Which shortcuts and handlers must a custom interactive node get that standard controls already have?
cards.extra: Built-in controls arrive with keyboard behaviour; a custom node does not. If it matters to the user, key handling must be added deliberately.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle;
class Seat {
    Rectangle node = new Rectangle();
    Seat() { node.setFocusTraversable(true); node.setOnKeyPressed(e -> toggle()); }
    void toggle() {}
}

cards.front: When UI state changes visually, what else should change?
cards.extra: A status label that only updates its pixels leaves the reader stale. Update accessibleText in the same code path as the visible change.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.Label status = new javafx.scene.control.Label("Idle");
status.setText("Saved");                              // the visual state changed
status.setAccessibleText("Saved: document saved");    // accessible text changes in the same code path
System.out.println(status.getText() + " / " + status.getAccessibleText());

cards.front: Package name, fx:controller value and FXML/CSS resource paths must all agree on what?
cards.extra: A mismatch doesn't fail at compile time; the loader throws at runtime. Aligning them keeps resource lookup predictable as the project grows.
cards.example:
package com.example.a11y;
public class AccessibleFxController { }
// fx:controller="com.example.a11y.AccessibleFxController"
// resources: com/example/a11y/form.fxml, com/example/a11y/base.css

cards.front: Which action gets a keyboard accelerator in the accessible form example, and why?
cards.extra: Accelerators give efficient keyboard-only operation to users who cannot use a mouse. Custom keyboard access on nodes plus shortcuts on actions cover both.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.control.MenuItem;
import javafx.scene.input.KeyCombination;
MenuItem save = new MenuItem("Save");
save.setAccelerator(KeyCombination.keyCombination("Ctrl+S")); // keyboard-only workflow

cards.front: Why declare dependencies in a module descriptor for an FXML app?
cards.extra: Spelling out requires javafx.controls and javafx.fxml (and opening the controller package) makes FXML loading and controller access predictable, and enforces architecture as the app grows.
cards.example:
module a11y.app {
    requires javafx.controls;
    requires javafx.fxml;
    opens com.example.a11y to javafx.fxml;
}

cards.front: Which three accessibility members are defined on javafx.scene.Node for talking to a screen reader?
cards.extra: The first two are overridden by your control to answer queries and perform actions. The third is called by your code to announce a change. Controls, shapes and canvas share them.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.Node;
Node n = new javafx.scene.control.Button();
n.queryAccessibleAttribute(javafx.scene.AccessibleAttribute.TEXT);
n.executeAccessibleAction(javafx.scene.AccessibleAction.FIRE);
n.notifyAccessibleAttributeChanged(javafx.scene.AccessibleAttribute.SELECTED);

cards.front: Who calls queryAccessibleAttribute?
cards.extra: It fires when assistive technology asks about the node; your override returns the requested information. Handle unknown attributes by delegating to super so default behaviour survives.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleAttribute;
class Seat extends javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle {
    @Override public Object queryAccessibleAttribute(AccessibleAttribute a, Object... p) {
        return super.queryAccessibleAttribute(a, p); // invoked by the FX accessibility bridge
    }
}

cards.front: Who calls notifyAccessibleAttributeChanged?
cards.extra: It tells the bridge that a value the screen reader may have cached is stale, so the tool can re-query it. Whereever the change originates, one call in the setter covers every input path.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleAttribute;
class Seat extends javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle {
    boolean selected;
    void setSelected(boolean v) { selected = v; notifyAccessibleAttributeChanged(AccessibleAttribute.SELECTED); }
}

cards.front: In an executeAccessibleAction override, what must you do for actions you do not handle?
cards.extra: The Node contract requires superclass delegation for unhandled queries and actions, so generic behaviour such as focus handling keeps working. Swallow them and the control seems broken to assistive tech.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleAction;
class Seat extends javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle {
    @Override public void executeAccessibleAction(AccessibleAction a, Object... p) {
        super.executeAccessibleAction(a, p); // superclass handles actions we ignore
    }
}

cards.front: What does AccessibleAttribute name?
cards.back: A piece of information about a node (TEXT, SELECTED…)
cards.extra: The bridge passes one when querying; your override switches on it and returns the matching value. Some attributes take parameters, e.g. an item lookup needs an index.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleAttribute;
AccessibleAttribute text = AccessibleAttribute.TEXT;
AccessibleAttribute selected = AccessibleAttribute.SELECTED;

cards.front: What does AccessibleAction name?
cards.back: An operation requested by assistive tech (FIRE, EXPAND…)
cards.extra: It is the input side, the counterpart to queryable attributes. Your override performs the action against the control's existing state.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleAction;
AccessibleAction fire = AccessibleAction.FIRE;
AccessibleAction expand = AccessibleAction.EXPAND;

cards.front: What determines which attributes and actions a node must support?
cards.extra: Pick the role that matches the interaction, then implement the attributes and actions that role documents. The role is the contract, not an arbitrary label.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleRole;
class Seat extends javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle {
    Seat() { setAccessibleRole(AccessibleRole.TOGGLE_BUTTON); } // role fixes required TEXT, SELECTED, FIRE
}

cards.front: A toggleable seat should use which role, with which attributes and action?
cards.extra: SELECTED exposes on/off state, TEXT gives the reader its name, and FIRE is the activation the screen reader sends. The same role also tells the reader it toggles.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleRole;
class Seat extends javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle {
    Seat() { setAccessibleRole(AccessibleRole.TOGGLE_BUTTON); }
    // supports AccessibleAttribute.TEXT, .SELECTED and AccessibleAction.FIRE
}

cards.front: Where should an accessibility action apply selection rules?
cards.extra: Reject unavailable or disabled elements exactly as mouse and keyboard paths do. Otherwise a screen reader could bypass a rule that visual input cannot.
cards.example:
class Seat extends javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle {
    boolean available = true, selected;
    @Override public void executeAccessibleAction(javafx.scene.AccessibleAction a, Object... p) {
        if (a == javafx.scene.AccessibleAction.FIRE && available) { selected = !selected; }
    }
}

cards.front: Where should notifyAccessibleAttributeChanged be called for a selection change?
cards.extra: Placing it there covers clicks, Space/Enter, accessibility actions and a Clear button alike. One notification point, no path forgotten.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleAttribute;
class Seat extends javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle {
    boolean selected;
    void setSelected(boolean value) { selected = value; notifyAccessibleAttributeChanged(AccessibleAttribute.SELECTED); }
}

cards.front: Which API reports whether accessibility is active, and which property can you bind to?
cards.extra: Bind UI that only helps assistive tech — like a copyable summary — to the property so it appears the moment a screen reader starts, not at launch.
cards.example:
import javafx.application.Platform;
class A11yWatch {
    boolean active = Platform.isAccessibilityActive();
    void listen() { Platform.accessibilityActiveProperty().addListener((o,a,b) -> System.out.println(b)); }
}

cards.front: What does the AccessibleAttribute.DISABLED query report?
cards.back: Whether the node is unavailable or disabled
cards.extra: Return true when the element cannot be operated, so the reader announces it as such. In the seat map that is an occupied seat or a disabled node.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleAttribute;
import javafx.scene.Node;
Node seat = new javafx.scene.control.Button();
seat.setDisable(true);
boolean disabled = (boolean) seat.queryAccessibleAttribute(AccessibleAttribute.DISABLED);

cards.front: Why keep unavailable elements focusable in a custom control?
cards.back: So keyboard users can inspect location and status
cards.extra: Focus and selection are separate: arrow keys move focus without selecting, and the reader announces why the element cannot be chosen. Defensive skipping hides information.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.Label item = new javafx.scene.control.Label("Unavailable");
item.setAccessibleText("Unavailable item, position 2 of 5");   // status and location for the reader
item.setFocusTraversable(true);   // stay reachable so keyboard users can inspect it
item.focus();                     // focus can land here without selecting the item
System.out.println(item.getAccessibleText());

cards.front: Reading accessibility information must have what side effect?
cards.extra: Queries are pure reads. If querying mutates state, a screen reader merely browsing the map would select seats, which is a serious usability bug.
cards.example:
import javafx.scene.AccessibleAttribute;
class Seat extends javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle {
    @Override public Object queryAccessibleAttribute(AccessibleAttribute a, Object... p) {
        return super.queryAccessibleAttribute(a, p); // read-only: no selection, no focus move
    }
}

cards.front: What does the javac compiler turn a .java file into?
cards.extra: Bytecode is binary aimed at the JVM instruction set, not at your CPU, which is why one compiled artifact runs on any machine with a suitable JVM.
cards.example:
javac HelloWorld.java   # produces HelloWorld.class: bytecode
java HelloWorld         # runs that bytecode on the JVM

cards.text: A {{c1::public}} top-level class must live in a file named after it, with the {{c2::.java}} extension.
cards.extra: The compiler enforces the public-class rule, case included; a non-public class may use any legal file name. Plain text only — smart quotes from a word processor break compilation.
cards.example:
public class Ex {
    public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello World!"); }
}

cards.front: What case convention applies to Java source file names?
cards.back: Start with a capital letter (matching the class)
cards.extra: It is not enforced by the compiler beyond the public-class rule, but every convention follows it. The first character should be a letter; a word processor's smart quotes will break the file.
cards.example:
class MyFirstJavaApp {   // saved as MyFirstJavaApp.java: capital first letter, matching the class
    public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello, World!"); }
}

cards.front: What is the exact signature of the main method the launcher looks for?
cards.extra: Public so the launcher can call it, static so no instance is needed, void because there is no return value, and a String array parameter — the entry point Java starts from.
cards.example:
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("entry point"); }
}

cards.front: What is the JAVA_HOME environment variable meant to point to?
cards.extra: Tools and build systems read it to locate the JDK; bin is appended to find javac and java. PATH is separate — it must contain that bin directory for the bare commands to resolve.
cards.example:
export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/jdk   # root directory of the JDK
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH

cards.front: JDK vs JRE — what can the JRE not do?
cards.extra: The JRE held the JVM and libraries needed to run an app but had no compiler. It is no longer distributed by OpenJDK or Oracle, so downloading 'Java' today means the JDK.
cards.example:
java MyFirstJavaApp         # runtime only: the JRE can run bytecode but cannot compile
javac MyFirstJavaApp.java   # compiler: available in the JDK, not the JRE

cards.front: What does the error telling you the launcher cannot find MyFirstJavaApp usually mean?
cards.extra: The source-launcher form is java MyFirstJavaApp.java. Dropping the extension makes the launcher look for a compiled class with that name instead.
cards.example:
java MyFirstJavaApp.java   // correct
java MyFirstJavaApp        // error: cannot find MyFirstJavaApp - .java suffix omitted

cards.front: Syntax error vs semantic error at compile time — give the classic trigger of each?
cards.extra: The parser rejects malformed code and reports line and column. Past parsing, the compiler still checks correctness — like definite assignment — and refuses to compile.
cards.example:
int x = 1                              // syntax error: ';' expected
int y;                                 // semantic error: y may not have been initialized
System.out.println(y);

cards.front: Since which Java SE version can the java launcher run a .java file without a separate compile step?
cards.extra: The launcher compiles in memory and runs the result, collapsing the two steps. From Java SE 22 it can also resolve a program spread over several source files.
cards.example:
javac HelloWorld.java && java HelloWorld    // classic: compile, then run
java HelloWorld.java                        // since Java SE 11: no separate compile step

cards.front: What kind of files does the JDK's compiler produce, and are they human-readable?
cards.extra: Source is written for people; class files are for the machine. javac performs the transformation, and a source error prevents any class file being written.
cards.example:
javac MyFirstJavaApp.java
// produces MyFirstJavaApp.class - binary bytecode, not human-readable
java MyFirstJavaApp

cards.front: Which two tools from the JDK perform compilation and execution respectively?
cards.extra: javac turns source into class files; the java launcher starts the JVM with those classes. Both live in the JDK's bin directory, which must be on PATH.
cards.example:
javac MyFirstJavaApp.java   # javac compiles source
java MyFirstJavaApp         # java executes the compiled program

cards.front: When you set JAVA_HOME and PATH in a shell, what happens on closing it?
cards.back: The variables are lost with the shell
cards.extra: Shell environment changes are per-session; a new terminal starts clean. Make them persistent by editing the shell profile, not by retyping them in each window.
cards.example:
export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/jdk
# closing the shell loses JAVA_HOME and PATH changes; set them again in a new shell
