cards.front: What does jshell stand for in practice — what loop does it run?
cards.extra: It reads a snippet, evaluates it, prints the result, and repeats — ideal for learning syntax, probing APIs, and prototyping before writing a class.
cards.example:
jshell                 // read-eval-print loop: read, evaluate, print, repeat
jshell> 1 + 2

cards.front: What does jshell do with a snippet that is missing its terminating semicolon?
cards.extra: A complete snippet is evaluated once the input reads as finished; the tool appends the missing terminator so quick prototyping stays frictionless.
cards.example:
jshell> int answer = 42
// jshell automatically adds the missing terminating semicolon

cards.front: In jshell, what does the /vars command list?
cards.extra: Siblings exist for other snippet kinds: /methods for methods, /types for classes and interfaces, /list for all snippets with their IDs.
cards.example:
jshell> int count = 3;
jshell> /vars
// lists each variable's name, type and value

cards.front: Which jshell command shows every snippet with its ID, including failed and dropped ones?
cards.extra: Startup snippets get IDs beginning with s and failed snippets IDs beginning with e. Without -all only active snippets are shown.
cards.example:
jshell> /list -all
// every snippet with its ID, including failed and dropped ones

cards.front: How do you drop a snippet in jshell, and what does dropping do?
cards.extra: You can pass a name, an ID or an ID range with a hyphen. Dependencies on dropped snippets become invalid, which usually surfaces immediately as an error.
cards.example:
jshell> /list
1 : int x = 3;
jshell> /drop 1
jshell> /list       // snippet 1 is inactive

cards.front: jshell /reset vs /reload?
cards.extra: Reset discards all entered code. Reload restarts the session, reruns startup scripts, and silently replays the valid history, so prior work survives a restart.
cards.example:
jshell> /reset     // restart: history is not replayed
jshell> /reload    // restart: history is replayed in order

cards.front: What does the /save command write, and where?
cards.extra: By default active snippets are saved; -all includes startup, failed and overwritten ones, and -history saves the sequential input log. The file can later be loaded with /open.
cards.example:
jshell> /save snippets.jsh
// writes snippets and commands to the file snippets.jsh

cards.front: Which predefined jshell script defines print, println and printf as methods?
cards.extra: DEFAULT loads common imports, JAVASE imports every Java SE package, and TOOLING defines methods to drive javac, jar and friends from inside the shell.
cards.example:
jshell PRINTING
// predefined script defines print, println and printf as jshell methods

cards.front: Which /exit argument supplies the process exit status?
cards.extra: With no argument the status is 0. If the snippet's result is not an integer or errors, the tool reports it and stays open — useful for scripting jshell in pipelines.
cards.example:
jshell> /exit 3
// argument is an integer expression snippet; process exits with status 3

cards.front: Which jshell feedback modes exist, and which is the default?
cards.back: verbose, normal, concise, silent, custom — default normal
cards.extra: Switch at startup with --feedback or -v/-q/-s, or inside a session with /set feedback. Errors are reported in every mode.
cards.example:
jshell --feedback normal    // default
/set feedback verbose
/set feedback concise
/set feedback silent
/set mode mymode normal     // custom

cards.front: Which flag makes jshell read from standard input, fitting into a pipe chain?
cards.back: A hyphen (-) in place of load-files
cards.extra: That suppresses interactive I/O. It turns jshell into a filter, so a stream of statements can be piped in and its results examined.
cards.example:
echo 'System.out.println("piped");' | jshell -
# a hyphen for load-files makes jshell read snippets from standard input

cards.front: Which keystroke converts an expression into a variable declaration of the inferred type?
cards.extra: Shift+M converts an expression or statement into a method declaration, and Shift+I offers imports for an identifier that does not resolve.
cards.example:
jshell> 2 + 3
// Shift+V converts the expression into a declaration of the inferred type (int)

cards.front: Which jshell command abbreviation is invalid, and why?
cards.extra: Unique prefixes work, e.g. /l for /list. For the ambiguous ones use /se for /set and /sa for /save. Subcommands and options accept abbreviations too.
cards.example:
jshell> /s     // invalid: ambiguous between /set and /save
jshell> /se    // unique abbreviation for /set
jshell> /sa    // unique abbreviation for /save

cards.front: With 15 snippets entered, which one does /-4 rerun?
cards.extra: /-n counts n back from the most recent, and /-1 is the last one. Commands are excluded from the count, so typing /list between snippets does not shift the numbering.
cards.example:
// 15 snippets entered (IDs 1 through 15)
jshell> /-4    // reruns the 11th snippet

cards.front: Where does the result of an expression go when no variable is assigned?
cards.extra: jshell creates one automatically and shows its value, so you need not name it. It is a real variable and appears in /vars afterwards.
cards.example:
jshell> 2 + 3
// result goes into a scratch variable because no variable was assigned

cards.front: In which environment variables does jshell look for an external editor?
cards.extra: The first match wins. Among these, JSHELLEDITOR takes precedence, then VISUAL, then EDITOR; if none is set, a simple built-in editor opens.
cards.example:
JSHELLEDITOR=vi jshell   # external editor: checked first
VISUAL=code jshell       # then VISUAL
EDITOR=nano jshell       # then EDITOR

cards.front: Which flag disables jshell's startup scripts, and which flag conflicts with it?
cards.extra: Use --no-startup to begin with nothing preloaded, or to run only scripts named on the command line. Jshell refuses the combination of both.
cards.example:
jshell --no-startup
# disables startup scripts; cannot be combined with --startup

cards.front: What do startup scripts do in jshell, and when do they rerun?
cards.back: Preload code/imports at start; rerun on /reset, /reload, /env
cards.extra: Default startup snippets are imports of common packages, hence s-prefixed IDs. The rerun matters: a restart replays your environment rather than starting from zero.
cards.example:
jshell --startup DEFAULT   # startup scripts preload imports/code when jshell starts
jshell> /reset             # they rerun on /reset, /reload and /env

cards.front: Which flag adds root modules when jshell resolves the module graph?
cards.extra: It works at startup and in /env, /reset, /reload. Modules and classpath both apply: --module-path says where modules live, --class-path says where class files are.
cards.example:
jshell --add-modules java.sql
// adds java.sql as a root module while resolving the module graph

cards.front: For a single-file source program, which class must contain main?
cards.back: The first class defined in the file
cards.extra: The launcher scans to find the entry point; if no class in the file declares main, the launch fails. Other classes may follow in any order.
cards.example:
class First { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("first class runs"); } }
class Second { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("not the entry point"); } }
// java SourceFile.java: the first class defined in the file must contain main

cards.front: Which JEP added multi-file source-code launching, and in which JDK?
cards.extra: It lets the launcher compile and run a program spread over several .java files, giving a gradual step up from one-file experiments to real projects.
cards.example:
// JEP 458: Launch Multi-File Source-Code Programs (JDK 22)
java Main.java    // launcher locates, compiles and loads the other source files

cards.front: For multi-file launching, where must the source files live relative to the main class?
cards.extra: A class model.Person must sit in model/Person.java beside the main class. When the layout matches the packages, the launcher finds, compiles and loads them.
cards.example:
// model/Person.java          -> package model;
// service/PersonService.java -> package service;
java Main.java    // launcher finds model/ and service/ beside Main.java

cards.front: Which classes must be put on the classpath for a source-launched program?
cards.extra: Core JDK classes such as Scanner or MatchResult resolve without a classpath. A third-party library such as Apache Commons Lang's RandomUtils needs its JAR added explicitly.
cards.example:
java Main.java                      // JDK classes: no classpath entry needed
java -cp commons-lang.jar Main.java  // non-JDK classes: add the jar

cards.front: What must the first line of a shebang .java file contain?
cards.extra: It names the launcher, not the compiler. The file must not end in .java and must be chmod +x, then it can be run as a script on a Unix-like OS.
cards.example:
#!/path/to/your/bin/java --source 27
// first line of a shebang file: java launcher with --source version; no .java extension

cards.front: A shebang Java script reads arguments — what happens if none are supplied?
cards.extra: The script indexes into args assuming an argument exists, so a bare run throws. Check args.length before touching the array in real scripts.
cards.example:
String[] args = new String[0];   // shebang script launched with no command-line arguments
System.out.println("Hello " + args[0]);   // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

cards.front: Why use source-code launching at all?
cards.extra: The launcher compiles in memory automatically, so one command runs the file. It is great for trying language features and API calls, less suited to shipping applications.
cards.example:
javac HelloWorld.java && java HelloWorld   // explicit compile, then run
java HelloWorld.java                       // source launching: skip explicit compilation

cards.front: Can a single-file source program still receive command-line arguments?
cards.extra: Anything after the file name lands in main's String[] exactly as for a compiled class, so testing argument handling needs no extra setup.
cards.example:
class HelloJava { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello " + args[0]); } }
// java HelloJava.java World!   ->  args[0] is "World!" from the command line

cards.front: What is an Eclipse workspace?
cards.extra: Chosen when Eclipse starts, it scopes the projects, settings and metadata you can see. Switching workspace switches the set of projects entirely.
cards.example:
// An Eclipse workspace is the directory holding most of your projects
java.nio.file.Path workspace = java.nio.file.Path.of("C:/dev/workspace");
java.nio.file.Path project = workspace.resolve("my-project");   // a project under it

cards.front: What is Eclipse's built-in completion feature called, and what trigger key does it use?
cards.extra: It completes class and method names and also expands idiom shorthands such as sysout. Suggestions are confirmed with Enter or a double-click.
cards.example:
// Eclipse Content Assist is triggered with Ctrl+Space
String msg = "hello";
msg.toUpperCase();   // a completion proposal from Content Assist

cards.front: What does Content Assist's sysout expansion produce?
cards.extra: Entry of main plus Ctrl+Space similarly offers the main method skeleton. These are template expansions, not textual edits to your source.
cards.example:
class Demo {
    void demo() { System.out.println(); }   // Content Assist expands sysout to System.out.println();
}

cards.front: What list does Eclipse use to collect every compile error and warning in the workspace?
cards.extra: Errors also appear underlined in red in the editor, with Quick Fix suggestions on hover. Warnings flag code that compiles but is likely wrong or pointless.
cards.example:
// Eclipse: Window > Show View > Problems
// the Problems view collects every compile error and warning in the workspace

cards.front: Eclipse offers a Quick Fix for an error — should you accept it blindly?
cards.back: No — several fixes exist, only one matches your intent
cards.extra: Adds an unused import, declares a variable, or something else entirely: an IDE cannot know intent. The cheapest way to a new bug is pressing the first suggestion.
cards.example:
// Eclipse Quick Fix offers several proposals; choose the one matching intent
int n = Integer.parseInt("42");   // String -> int: parse is the matching fix
// Integer.valueOf("42") is another proposal, not the same intent here

cards.front: Eclipse's Refactor ▸ Rename differs from a text replace how?
cards.back: It updates every reference to the symbol
cards.extra: The rename is semantic and scoped to the symbol, so same-named strings and comments are left alone, and bindings that would break are flagged. Ensure you rename the code, not just the typo you spotted.
cards.example:
class Person { String firstName = "Ada"; String greet() { return "Hello " + firstName; } }
// Refactor > Rename firstName to givenName rewrites the field and its reference, unlike text replace

cards.front: What method set does Eclipse's Source ▸ Generate Getters and Setters produce?
cards.extra: Generate hashCode() and equals() and Generate toString() work the same way. Records are often preferable, but the generator helps on legacy or mutable classes.
cards.example:
class Person { // Source > Generate Getters and Setters for selected fields
    private String firstName; private int age;
    public String getFirstName() { return firstName; }
    public void setFirstName(String firstName) { this.firstName = firstName; }
    public int getAge() { return age; } public void setAge(int age) { this.age = age; }
}

cards.front: Eclipse run mode vs debug mode regarding breakpoints?
cards.extra: Debug mode suspends at each hit breakpoint and switches you to the Debug perspective, where the Variables view lists current values.
cards.example:
// Eclipse Run mode: all breakpoints are ignored
int x = 1;   // a breakpoint on this line does not suspend in Run mode
System.out.println(x);

cards.front: In the Eclipse Debug perspective, what does a line shown with a green background mark?
cards.extra: Use it to reason about what comes next, then Step Over (F6) to advance one line within the current method, Step Into (F5) to descend, or Resume (F8) to continue.
cards.example:
int a = 1;   // green background in Debug perspective: next statement to execute
int b = 2;   // not executed yet
System.out.println(a + b);

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::15 Getting Started::02 Using IDEs

cards.front: In IntelliJ, which shortcut steps into a method?
cards.extra: Stepping over a line is F8. IntelliJ's default debugger keys mirror the latter half of the classic set, whereas Eclipse binds into=5 / over=6 / resume=8.
cards.example:
class StepInto {                      // IntelliJ F7 steps into the callee
    void outer() { inner(); }         // F7 at this call enters inner()
    void inner() { System.out.println("inside"); }
}

cards.front: What is a compact source file in Java 25?
cards.back: A file with no class declaration, just code
cards.extra: It removes the boilerplate wrapping and gives you a runnable main by default. IntelliJ can convert one to a regular class via Alt+Enter or command completion.
cards.example:
// Java 25 compact source file: no class declaration, just code
// System.out.println("Hello");   // the whole file is this statement
// java Main.java prints Hello

cards.front: What does IntelliJ's Run/Debug configuration let you change about a launch?
cards.back: Program arguments, VM options, env vars, working dir
cards.extra: What belongs in the run configuration is anything default settings cannot express about a particular launch, rather than in code.
cards.example:
String programArgs = "input.txt";   // Program arguments
String vmOptions = "-Xmx512m";        // VM options
String envVar = "LANG=C";             // Environment variables
String workingDir = "C:/work";        // Working directory

cards.front: Evaluating sum / numbers.length in a debugger with an empty int array throws which exception?
cards.extra: The int division performs the / before the cast; the empty array's length is 0. Casting earlier to double, like (double) sum / numbers.length, divides by 0.0 and yields NaN (not an exception).
cards.example:
int sum = 0;
int[] numbers = {};   // empty int array, watched in the debugger
System.out.println(sum / numbers.length);   // ArithmeticException: / by zero

cards.front: A test expects 0 as the average of an empty array but gets NaN. Which arithmetic produced it?
cards.extra: In floating point, 0.0/0.0 is NaN, not an exception. The lesson in the example: NaN fails an equality assertion because NaN is not equal to anything, itself included.
cards.example:
int[] numbers = {};   // empty array: the average test sums no elements
float sum = 0f;
float average = sum / numbers.length;   // 0.0f / 0 gives NaN
System.out.println(average);

cards.front: What is Search Everywhere, and its trigger?
cards.back: Search files, settings and actions — double Shift
cards.extra: Tabs narrow the scope to Classes, Files, Symbols, Actions or Text. Find in Files (Ctrl+Shift+F / ⌘⇧F) searches content and can narrow to module, directory or scope.
cards.example:
// press Shift twice  ->  Search Everywhere
// searches files, settings and actions; Tab selects Classes, Files, Symbols, Actions or Text

cards.front: In IntelliJ on Windows/Linux, which shortcut runs the current file?
cards.extra: Running the file in focus is distinct from running the run configuration, whose keystroke is Shift+F10 on Windows/Linux.
cards.example:
// IntelliJ Windows/Linux: Ctrl+F10 runs the current file (macOS: ⌃R)
class CurrentFile {
    public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("current file ran"); }
}

cards.front: Where does IntelliJ place a newly generated test class?
cards.extra: Maven's layout keeps tests separate from production code. The Generate Tests picker also writes the imports for the chosen test library.
cards.example:
String testSourceRoot = "src/test/java";   // IntelliJ puts generated tests here
java.nio.file.Path generated = java.nio.file.Path.of(testSourceRoot, "MyTest.java");
System.out.println(generated);   // src/test/java/MyTest.java

cards.front: What does IntelliJ's Evaluate Expression let you do at a breakpoint?
cards.back: Evaluate expressions and change their values in the paused frame — not arbitrary code injection
cards.extra: You can call methods on in-scope variables and read the result before the program moves. That is how sum / numbers.length was pinned to a division by zero.
cards.example:
int sum = 0; int[] numbers = new int[0];
double pausedFrameValue = numbers.length == 0 ? 0 : (double) sum / numbers.length; // Evaluate Expression in the paused frame

cards.front: In IntelliJ, which shortcut renames a class, variable or method?
cards.extra: Extract variable is Ctrl+Alt+V and extract method Ctrl+Alt+M on Windows/Linux. Every refactoring should be followed by a test run.
cards.example:
int oldName = 1;   // IntelliJ Shift+F6 (macOS ⇧F6) renames variables, methods, classes
int renamed = oldName;
System.out.println(renamed);

cards.front: Which extension enables Java development in VS Code per dev.java?
cards.extra: It is on the VS Code Marketplace and brings project creation, building via Maven/Gradle, debugging, refactoring and testing into the editor.
cards.example:
code --install-extension Oracle.oracle-java
// the Oracle Java Platform Extension enables Java development in VS Code

cards.front: In VS Code, where can the launch and debugger configurations be customised?
cards.extra: Default launch configurations live there; the Run and Debug view's Run Configuration panel edits arguments, VM options, environment variables and working directory.
cards.example:
{
  "configurations": [{ "type": "java", "name": "Launch Main", "mainClass": "Concatenate" }]
}
// launch.json: customise launch and debugger configurations here

cards.front: What is the VS Code Project Explorer provided by the extension?
cards.extra: It layers Maven/Gradle awareness over the plain file explorer, so you can clean, compile, test, debug and run by project rather than by folder.
cards.example:
java.nio.file.Path src = java.nio.file.Path.of("src/main/java/com/example/app");
System.out.println(src);   // Project Explorer shows packages as this tree
String[] packages = {"com.example.app", "com.example.app.model"};

cards.front: Which JDK does the Oracle Java Platform Extension require at minimum?
cards.extra: Both the extension and its debugger support JDK 11 and newer — so the debugger cannot target pre-modular JDK 8 runtimes.
cards.example:
int minJdk = 11;   // Oracle Java Platform Extension requires JDK 11 at minimum
System.out.println(minJdk >= 11 ? "supported" : "too old");

cards.front: Which settings do you edit to point the extension at another JDK?
cards.extra: The extension checks jdk.jdkhome, then java.home, JDK_HOME, JAVA_HOME, and finally the system path. A per-version profile can override jdk.jdkhome in its own settings.
cards.example:
{
  "jdk.jdkhome": "/path/to/another/jdk"
}
// VS Code user settings JSON: point the extension at another JDK

cards.front: How do you attach the VS Code debugger to a running JVM?
cards.back: Pick the process or a JDWP port
cards.extra: A configured JDWP listener lets the debugger connect to a JVM already running. On Windows, Attach to Shared Memory is offered as an additional route.
cards.example:
String byProcess = "running JVM from the process picker";   // VS Code attach option
String byPort = "JDWP port";                                 // other attach option
System.out.println(byProcess + " or " + byPort);

cards.front: What does VS Code's source action for JavaDoc generate?
cards.extra: Typing /** above a method signature offers to complete it, with tags for parameters and return already in place. The parser does the tedious part.
cards.example:
class Doc {
    /** pre-populated JavaDoc comment from the VS Code source action */
    static int area(int width, int height) { return width * height; }
}

cards.front: A generated test method is empty or failing — how do you keep it from running?
cards.extra: That skips the test until you implement it, so the suite isn't permanently red. Replace it by writing assertions as soon as you know the expected behaviour.
cards.example:
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Disabled;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
@Disabled
class ConcatenateTest { @Test void emptyTest() { } }

cards.front: What is the role of pom.xml for a Maven project?
cards.extra: It states coordinates, dependencies, plugins and build settings. VS Code and IntelliJ both generate a starter pom.xml when creating a Maven project.
cards.example:
// Maven: pom.xml is the single build configuration file
// <project><modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion> ... </project>
// dependencies, plugins and properties all live in that one file

cards.front: What refactoring does the extension offer for get(0) on Java 21+?
cards.extra: Similarly get(size()-1) becomes getLast(). The replacement expresses intent instead of arithmetic, which is why the collection API added them.
cards.example:
java.util.List<String> names = java.util.List.of("Ada", "Grace");
String first = names.get(0);   // VS Code quick fix on Java 21+
String modern = names.getFirst();   // SequencedCollection.getFirst()
System.out.println(first.equals(modern));   // true

cards.front: What is a breakpoint?
cards.back: A marker that pauses the program at a line
cards.extra: It tells the debugger to suspend execution there, freezing the state so you can inspect variables and step through from that point.
cards.example:
int value = 7;   // a breakpoint is a marker that pauses the program at this line
System.out.println(value);

cards.front: What happens to breakpoints when you run in normal (non-debug) mode?
cards.extra: The VM only suspends for breakpoints under a debug launch. Running normally is faster precisely because no debug hooks are installed.
cards.example:
// Normal (non-debug) run: breakpoints are ignored
int x = 3;   // this line's breakpoint has no effect
System.out.println(x);

cards.front: What does step into do?
cards.back: Executes, entering the first line of the callee
cards.extra: You land inside the called method so you can watch its internals. Use it when the bug might be in the method being invoked.
cards.example:
class StepInto2 {
    static int twice(int n) { return n + n; }
    static void run() { int r = twice(3); System.out.println(r); }   // Step Into enters twice()
}

cards.front: What does step over do?
cards.extra: The whole call is treated as one step, so you stay in the current method. Prefer it when the callee is known-good or not relevant.
cards.example:
class StepOver {
    static int twice(int n) { return 2 * n; }
    static void run() { int d = twice(4); System.out.println(d); }   // Step Over stays in run()
}

cards.front: What does step out (step return) do?
cards.back: Runs to the end of the current method
cards.extra: Control returns to the caller with the method's result. Some IDEs call it step return; the behaviour is the same.
cards.example:
class StepOut {
    static int inner() { return 5; }   // Step Out runs to the end of this method
    static void outer() { int x = inner(); System.out.println(x); }
}

cards.front: What does resume do?
cards.back: Continues until the next breakpoint or exit
cards.extra: Use it to skip over code that has already been verified. It stops early only if another breakpoint is hit.
cards.example:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {   // Resume continues to the next breakpoint
    System.out.println(i);     // or to program exit if none is reached
}

cards.front: What is a conditional breakpoint?
cards.back: A breakpoint that suspends only when a condition is true
cards.extra: You attach a Java expression and the debugger evaluates it on each arrival. In a loop it stops only on the interesting iteration, saving repeated resumes.
cards.example:
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {   // breakpoint condition: i == 3
    System.out.println(i);      // suspends only when the condition is true
}

cards.front: What does the debugger's Evaluate facility allow at a breakpoint?
cards.extra: You can call methods on in-scope variables and inspect the result. This makes it an interactive probe rather than a passive viewer.
cards.example:
int total = 4;   // at a breakpoint, Evaluate runs Java against live state
System.out.println(total * 2 + 1);   // arbitrary expression over total

cards.front: What does changing data in the debugger let you test?
cards.back: The effect of a value without editing code
cards.extra: Overwrite a variable and let execution continue, which is a cheap way to preview a candidate fix before committing it to source.
cards.example:
int threshold = 10;   // in the debugger, change this value while suspended
boolean passes = 4 >= threshold;
System.out.println(passes);   // test the effect without editing the code

cards.front: When the debugger shows the call stack, what does each entry represent?
cards.back: A method call that led to that point
cards.extra: You can click a frame to inspect the variables in scope for that call, which traces the path of execution rather than guessing it.
cards.example:
class StackDemo {
    static void leaf() { throw new RuntimeException("stack"); }   // entry: leaf()
    static void middle() { leaf(); }                              // entry: middle()
    static void root() { middle(); }                              // entry: root()
}

cards.front: Why prefer a debugger over println in a big program?
cards.extra: Output scatters through logs, needs cleanup, and re-running for a new question means editing code. A debugger asks fresh questions against the same run.
cards.example:
// println debugging scatters output statements through a big program
System.out.println("x=1");   // output noise, plus edits to add and remove it
System.out.println("x=2");   // a debugger inspects state without those edits

cards.front: What does a unit test do that a debugger cannot, and vice versa?
cards.back: Tests detect a wrong value; the debugger explains why
cards.extra: Until then, a test tells you a value is wrong; the debugger shows why inside the method. Tests then guard the fix against regression.
cards.example:
int actual = 3;
if (actual != 4) throw new AssertionError("expected 4, got " + actual); // test detects wrong value
// the debugger explains why actual became 3

cards.front: Where does the term debugging come from?
cards.extra: Grace Hopper's log popularised 'bug' for a defect. The word stuck even though the bugs today are our own logic.
cards.example:
// "debugging" comes from a moth found inside a computer in the 1940s
String origin = "a moth in the computer";
System.out.println(origin);   // hence debugging a program
